practice.title: Deepen the Understanding of Karma
agreedSteps: Keep our regret going over the week ahead — maintain the wish to purify and try to deepen the understanding of karma in some practical and beneficial way.
Move the practice forward: each one of us can bring our own approach to thinking about karma more deeply.
steps: Strengthen the wire between harm we create and harm we receive. When something unpleasant happens, practice asking: why did this happen to me and not to others? Try to arrive at the answer of karma rather than outer conditions.

Notice where guilt creeps in and distinguish it from virtuous regret. Guilt lives in the past and grasps at an identity of being a bad person. Regret faces forward — it's the wish to purify negative karma before it ripens.

Watch for non-virtuous regret — regretting virtuous actions like joining TTP, attending a puja, or taking vows. When unhappiness arises during practice, don't blame the practice. Unhappiness is coming from negative karma, not from the virtuous thing we're doing.
Use difficulty in practice as fuel: when virtue is hard and non-virtue is easy, treat that as proof of karmic inheritance that needs purifying, not as a reason for discouragement.
practice.quote: Harmful actions, harmful results — therefore I need to purify. Not harmful actions, harmful results — therefore I'm a big-time loser.

commentary.title: Wiring Harm We Create to Harm We Receive
content: The whole thing is actually quite simple. Harm we create and harm we receive — these two points usually aren't linked with a line between them in our mind. A big part of purification is just rewiring those two points to each other. If we do that over and over and make that wire completely linked, then the rest of the practice will follow.

Even as a baby, we're trying to figure out why we receive harm. We wire things: eat this food, feel awful. Be around that bully, get hurt. Too hot, too cold. We're making connections all day. But Buddha is offering a slightly different idea — all those things maybe are related in some way, but they're just conditions. The harm we receive is always linked to the karma we've created. The harm we've created.

One useful question to ponder: why did it happen to me, but not to others? The more we probe into the usual answers — genetics, something someone said — the less satisfying they are. They're just conditions, not the actual cause. The cause is karma.

commentary.title: Regret vs. Guilt: The Match Analogy
content: It is important not to misunderstand what it means to regret our unskillful actions. We should not view the suffering we experience as an externally applied punishment for our sins. Nor is it necessary to feel guilty, thinking we have offended some authority or force that is prepared to take revenge upon us. True regret is not concerned with such extraneous attitudes.

MTB gives a perfect analogy: a boy's parents prohibit him from playing with matches. He does so anyway and burns his finger. The proper response is for the child to regret his carelessness and learn to avoid similar dangers. An exaggerated response is for the child to think the match deliberately punished him for disobeying his parents. Such a superstitious reaction introduces extraneous considerations, such as guilt, that might reduce rather than increase his ability to deal with future dangerous situations intelligently.

Four students offered complementary explanations for why guilt reduces that ability. First, guilt makes it too much about the self — internalizing what should just be a simple cause-and-effect lesson. Second, guilt creates self-grasping: I am a bad person — a judgment that makes the negative karma feel like something that can't be removed. Third, this self-grasping reinforces a delusion that repeats the cycle. Fourth, introducing an external authority — either the authority is happy with you and it doesn't matter what you do, or the authority is unhappy with you and it doesn't matter what you do — weakens the link between actions and harm.

This is why living within the law of karma can be tricky. There's no one watching. And we know how to behave when there's a watcher. But there was never a watcher. It's just been karma the whole time.
commentary.quote: Touch fire, get burned — that's a completely different game than 'appease the authority, or at least just don't get caught.'

commentary.title: Three Types of Regret
content: From How to Understand the Mind, regret is one of the four changeable mental factors — it can be positive, negative, or neutral depending on how we approach it. The definition: a mental factor that feels remorse for actions done in the past.

Virtuous regret is developed by recognizing the faults and disadvantages of non-virtuous actions. We need to develop this regret for past negative actions before their effects have ripened. There is no point in feeling regret for actions whose effects have already ripened — once something has already ripened, that's about learning from it and accepting it patiently. Regret is about wanting to purify something. Guilt is living in the past. Regret is about action — I have negative karma that hasn't ripened yet, and I want to uproot it.

Non-virtuous regret is feeling regret for previously created virtuous actions — regretting having taken vows, being unhappy about commitments, regretting having made an offering. We should never develop such regrets. We don't want to blame the virtuous things we're doing for our unhappiness. That's miswiring what's going on — unhappiness is coming from negative karma, not from the virtuous practice. This non-virtuous regret can even make us not want to do positive things.

Neutral regret is very common — regretting having eaten unhealthy food, for example. It's generally better to avoid it because it can lead to unhappiness and serves no useful function. Before doing anything, we should carefully consider whether it's worthwhile. The wise person checks beforehand; the fool feels regret afterwards. If despite careful planning our actions do not succeed, there's no need to become unhappy or blame others — just recognize this is the result of past negative actions and willingly accept it.

commentary.title: Purifying Already-Ripened Karma
content: Fran raised an important question: if karma is continually ripening every moment, can we still purify the ongoing karma that's creating an ongoing issue, even though we can't undo the moment it ripened? KK confirmed this is correct.

The point is that a lot of guilt involves living in the past, thinking, 'This shouldn't have happened.' We can't reverse something from having happened through purification. But if there's something with continual negative karma ripening to maintain it, we can definitely purify that before the next moment ripens. The thoughts 'Why did I do that? I should have never done that' are incredibly pointless. They don't help us learn or change. Regret faces forward; guilt looks back.

commentary.title: Seeds, Imprints, and the Field of Consciousness
content: How is it that harmful results follow from harmful actions? It is through the force of an imprint placed on our mind that the potential to experience future suffering comes about. A person who commits murder plants a very strong negative impression on his own mind. Unless that impression is purified, the latent seed will remain in the mind, its power dormant but unimpaired. When appropriate circumstances are met, the seed will ripen as intense suffering.

The situation is analogous to an arid piece of ground into which seeds were planted long ago. As long as the seeds are not destroyed, they retain their potential to grow. Should the ground be watered sufficiently, the long-forgotten seeds will suddenly sprout. Our karmic actions plant seeds in the field of our consciousness. When we encounter the proper conditions, these seeds bear their karmic fruit.

The tomato-and-red-car analogy illustrates how we misidentify causes. A tomato plant ripens in the garden, and there's a red car parked outside. Our mind sees: tomato plant, red car — correlation. Next season: same pattern. But the tomato plant is really caused by the tomato seed, not the red car, not even the soil. This is what we do all the time — we see correlates and think they're causes. From Buddha's point of view, the non-karmic explanations are just as superstitious as thinking a rain dance made the rain come.

commentary.title: Acknowledging What We Already Have
content: From Modern Buddhism: from virtuous actions comes happiness, from non-virtuous actions comes suffering. If we believe in this, we believe in karma. We all already believe in this to some degree. We probably don't just lie, cheat, and steal willy-nilly even when no one's watching. That's because we already have this understanding.

When studying a topic, we need to acknowledge what we already have. We don't want to focus on moving forward thinking we don't have anything. We want to think: I'm moving it forward, acknowledging that I already have a lot. I just want to upgrade and refine my understanding.

commentary.title: Purifying Ordinary Appearances
content: Great Treasury of Merit presents purification from a tantric emptiness perspective. A mind filled with non-virtuous imprints cannot give rise to pure states of mind, because the cause is impure. If the mind itself is impure, the objects that appear to it will also be impure. Without purifying the mind, the pure appearances of generation stage and completion stage will be unattainable.

This means that when we go about our day and see an ordinary appearance — an inherently existent person, a suffering living being — that is actually negative karma ripening. It's the effect of our ordinary appearances and conceptions. This is very helpful to see: I have to purify that too. Just seeing people as ordinary and non-Buddhas — I've got to purify that.

commentary.title: Why Virtue Is Hard and Non-Virtue Is Easy
content: We've been accumulating negative actions since beginningless time, and the burden of this negativity weighs heavily upon us. We can know this simply by examining our experience: we can train in spiritual practices for a long time and accomplish almost no results, yet we can commit negative actions spontaneously, without any effort. Why? Because we've inherited from our previous lives a strong familiarity with non-virtue.

This is a reason people get discouraged — I'm trying to practice and it's so hard. But the teaching here is: use that as proof of the karmic inheritance that needs purifying. Oh, why is it easy to get angry but hard to be patient? That's just showing me the burden of negativity that's dragging me down. We can use those moments as a little fire, a little encouragement: I've got to purify.

commentary.title: Wrong Views and Teaching Dharma Skillfully
content: Wrong views constitute the heaviest and most damaging of all unskillful actions because they are directed inwardly and affect the perpetrator directly. One possible effect is an experience of great difficulty when later trying to study or meditate on the Dharma. This is why we can't push someone into understanding the Dharma. If they don't understand it, it's largely because of the negative karma arising in their mind.

This doesn't mean we use it as an excuse. The unskillful application would be using it to abdicate responsibility for the bad job we're doing — oh, it must just be their karma. That's a coping mechanism. The useful application is: when our approach becomes salesy or coercive, we can relax and accept the other person's journey. We help where we can, but we don't stubbornly try to make it work for someone where there's no traction.

There's a phrase that has germinated at the center: karma for ourself, compassion for others. The intention is good — don't use Dharma to judge someone or close your heart off. But we definitely should think about karma for others. Thinking about how they're trapped in the iron net of self-grasping, bound by the iron chains of karma, is actually a powerful way to develop compassion. We just need to be skillful. The practice from Geshe Chekawa: do not turn a god into a demon.
commentary.quote: We should definitely think about other people's karma. But we should also be skillful in what we say and what we teach.

dataShares.speaker: Anne K
dataShares.summary: Had a great experience purifying with her purification buddy — a real sense of lightness afterwards. But felt agitated when asked about meditation break practice, discovering she'd failed to do it amid too many simultaneous practices. KK pointed out that the agitation itself is the delusion, not the ambitious practice list, and encouraged seeing all practices as one integrated practice.

dataShares.speaker: Dale
dataShares.summary: Recovering from surgery, practice had been crappy or nonexistent. This morning sat down and did most of Heart Jewel — didn't have a great transformation but felt peaceful, and was happy with peaceful. Working to lock in the good stuff and slowly make his way back. Also asked about where negative thoughts that aren't acted on fall in the karma framework.

dataShares.speaker: Sumit
dataShares.summary: After last week's teaching skills class, doubled down on reading from Geshe-la's books. Got strong positive feedback — people couldn't even identify why the class felt different but said it was great. Started rereading New Essence of Vajrayana in preparation for the HYT summer. Takeaway: the power of Geshe-la's words is incredible.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Had a good week with ongoing cherishing-others practice combined with the daily Lamrim. But was jolted by KK's question about break practice — realized she tends to close the book on Sunday and not remember the specific TTP practice. A reminder not to be prideful about a good week when the specific assignment was forgotten.

dataShares.speaker: Kristin
dataShares.summary: Working through the promise piece of purification — how to choose something specific to promise when the scope is countless lives. Helpful to focus on practicing effort in the day. Also puzzled by the daily cycle: if purification practice at its conclusion imagines total purity, why purify again the next day? KK explained it as a correct belief on a valid base of imputation that drops when ordinary appearances return.

dataShares.speaker: Mimi
dataShares.summary: Started the week as a rotten log open to the sun, doing Vajrayogini purification. Then got called in by her boss about being late to work — colleagues had noticed. Was mortified and defensive, but recognized it as 'Buddha always delivers.' Apologized, took responsibility, and reframed it as part of confession and purification.
